kit.name: ELEGOO UNO R3 Super Starter Kit

identity.manufacturer: generic (SW-520D is a widely cloned part number/footprint; the datasheet fetched is from Bailin Electronics, sold under the 'Beelee' brand, but the same numbering is used by many manufacturers)
generic_equivalents: other 2-lead roll-ball tilt switches with the same footprint
identity.package: small cylindrical 2-lead through-hole switch, heat-shrink tube body

function.one_sentence_plain_english: A tiny sealed tube with metal balls inside that acts like a switch: closed one way up, open when tilted the other way.
function.what_it_is_used_for: Used as a crude orientation or motion sensor, for example to detect if something has been tipped over, shaken, or turned upside down.
function.how_it_works_briefly: Inside the small tube, two tiny conductive balls sit next to two contact pins. Held so the part's own 'upright' side faces down, gravity pulls the balls onto the contacts, closing the circuit. Tilt it far enough the other way (about 10 degrees one direction, about 45 degrees sideways, per the datasheet) and the balls roll away from the contacts, opening the circuit. It is a simple mechanical switch, not an electronic sensor, so it only reports 'past the tilt threshold' or not, never a precise angle.

pinout.name: Lead 1
pinout.role: one side of the internal ball-and-contact switch
pinout.notes: no fixed polarity; interchangeable with lead 2

pinout.name: Lead 2
pinout.role: other side of the internal ball-and-contact switch
pinout.notes: no fixed polarity; interchangeable with lead 1

pins.pin_1_identification: Both leads are electrically identical and interchangeable; there is no 'pin 1' polarity to find. What matters instead is physical orientation: per the manufacturer's diagram, tilting the body so the far (cap) end points down by more than 10 degrees opens the circuit, while tilting so the lead/pin end points down by more than 10 degrees closes it; held on its side, roughly 45 degrees of tilt is needed to change state.

electrical.operating_voltage: rated up to 12V per the manufacturer datasheet (a separate retailer's spec sheet for the same part number claims up to 24V; treat 12V as the better-sourced figure)
electrical.typical_current: well under the part's rating; normally wired through a pull-up/pull-down resistor into a digital input, so only a few mA flow at most
electrical.max_current: not explicitly stated in the fetched manufacturer datasheet; a separate retailer (Sunrom) lists switching current under 5 mA for the same part number
electrical.logic_level: simple dry contact; works fine at 3.3V or 5V logic since it is just a mechanical switch

key_specs.lead_size_mm: 0.6 diameter x 8 length, spaced 2.4 mm apart
key_specs.tilt_threshold: about 10 degrees tilting toward the cap or lead end; about 45 degrees tilting sideways (per manufacturer diagram)
key_specs.mechanical_life: rated in the tens of thousands of cycles by the manufacturer; sources vary between 50,000 and 100,000+

visual_identification.shape_and_size: Tiny black (sometimes gray) cylindrical tube, about 11.5 mm long and 5.2 mm across, like a small pill or capsule, with two thin bare metal legs (about 8 mm long) sticking straight out of one end.
visual_identification.color_and_markings: Plain black or gray heat-shrink tube body, no printed text or markings. You can sometimes hear or feel the tiny metal balls rattling faintly inside if you shake it.
visual_identification.printed_text_to_look_for: None; the part has no printed label.
easily_confused_with: a small electrolytic capacitor (similar cylindrical shape, but a capacitor is usually shinier or metal-cased and larger, this switch is noticeably shorter and thinner)
a small diode (similar 2-lead axial shape, but a diode is glass or plastic with a printed stripe and part number, this switch is a plain unmarked tube)

example_connections.uno_pin: GND (when using the pin's internal pull-up), or 5V with an external pull-down resistor to the digital pin

required_extra_parts: 10k ohm resistor for an external pull-up/pull-down, or use the UNO's built-in pull-up via pinMode(pin, INPUT_PULLUP) and skip the extra resistor
wiring_to_uno.arduino_library: none needed; read with the built-in digitalRead() function

hazards: none inherent; low voltage, low current, sealed part
handling_notes: do not crush or puncture the tube; it is sealed and not meant to be opened
mounting orientation matters: decide which way is 'up' for the project and test both tilt directions since the switch is not symmetric
common_mistakes: assuming it detects tilt equally in every direction, when per the datasheet it takes only about 10 degrees one way but about 45 degrees the other way or sideways
wiring only one lead, or leaving the input floating without a pull-up/pull-down resistor, causing random readings

symptoms_and_causes.symptom: input never changes no matter how the switch is tilted
symptoms_and_causes.likely_cause: one lead not actually connected, or the switch is mounted in an orientation where it never crosses its threshold angle
symptoms_and_causes.check: test continuity with a multimeter while manually tilting the part through a full range of angles

symptoms_and_causes.symptom: reading flickers or is unreliable right at the tilt point
symptoms_and_causes.likely_cause: this is a mechanical ball switch, so near the threshold angle it can bounce between open and closed; this is normal, not a fault
symptoms_and_causes.check: add simple debounce logic in code, or mount it well past the threshold in the intended resting orientation

troubleshooting.how_to_test_with_a_multimeter: Set the multimeter to continuity/beep mode and touch a probe to each lead. Slowly rotate the switch through different angles; it should beep (closed) in some orientations and go silent (open) in others, matching the manufacturer's tilt diagram.

confidence.notes: ELEGOO's kit lid lists a bare 'Tilt Ball Switch' with 2 pins (matching the seed data), not the 3-pin LM393 breakout module sold under the same SW-520D name; this record is priced and specified for the bare 2-lead part. The Bailin/Beelee datasheet fetched via TME.com is the primary source; it disagrees slightly with a secondary retailer's spec sheet (Sunrom) on maximum voltage and cycle life, so both figures are listed as uncertain rather than one being picked arbitrarily.
